      Abstract. This short note shows that the conventional (2-subset) bit-based division
      property trail search problem is NP-complete.
      Keywords: Cryptanalysis · Division property · NP-hardness



1    Introduction
Division property (DP) is a technique introduced by Todo in 2015 [Tod15]. Its goal is
finding integral distinguishers in symmetric-key primitives such as block ciphers or stream
ciphers. This technique was used to cryptanalyze full MISTY1 [BK16, Tod17].
    The technique is related to the algebraic representation of the cipher, meaning multi-
variate polynomials over the binary field F2 , where AND is the multiplication and XOR
is the addition. The high-level idea of the technique is to track ways in which a chosen
subset of input variables gets multiplied throughout the computation of the primitive.
Original division property, also referred to as 2-subset DP or conventional DP, simply
decides whether the selected inputs can in principle be multiplied or not; it does not
take into account possible XOR-cancellations of the product. Later, [TM16] proposed the
3-subset DP which tracks some of the possible cancellations. Finally, [HLM+ 20] showed
how to track all possible cancellations by counting the parity, and called the technique
“3-subset DP without the unknown subset”, which was also called monomial prediction
in [HSWW20].
    We focus on the bit-based variant introduced in [TM16], as opposed to word-level/state-
level division property [Tod15], which are easier to evaluate due to smaller state size
(depending on the word size). Xiang, Zhang, Bao, and Lin showed in [XZBL16] how to
use mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) solvers to efficiently apply the conventional
bit-based division property application to multiple block ciphers. One of the key ideas
here was representing the technique in terms of a trail search problem (see Section 2). The
surprising efficiency and generality of this method led to many further results, including
adaptations to the stronger division property variants: 3-subset DP [WHG+ 19], monomial
prediction [HSWW20]. These adaptations come at a large performance and complexity
penalty, since the problem reduces to parity counting of a given Boolean circuit [DRS24]
(⊕P -complete problem), which is believed to be hard, although not proven to be NP-hard.
Specific optimizations and tricks are needed for applying the perfect DP variant. And still,
many large instances are not feasible to be tested.

2                    Conventional bit-based division property trail search is NP-complete


Our contribution This note revisits the conventional (2-subset) bit-based division property
and its computational hardness. Despite its successful performance in cryptanalysis of many
primitives, we show that the underlying division trail search/existence problem (defined
as in [XZBL16]) is NP-complete, via a simple classical-style reduction from CNF-SAT.
This shows that even the basic division property variant cannot be evaluated for arbitrary
circuits in polynomial time (unless P=NP), and its success in practice is likely attributed
to a specific structure of targets, such as narrow circuit width (block size) and/or slow
diffusion.


2     Two-subset division property
Definition 1 (AND-XOR circuit). A circuit with AND and XOR gates is a directed
acyclic graph C = (V, E) with nodes V = I ∪ X ∪ A ∪ O corresponding respectively to
input gates I (indegree zero), XOR gates X, AND gates A, output gates O (indegree one,
outdegree zero).

Definition 2 (Division trail [XZBL16]). A division trail over an AND-XOR circuit
                                                    I∪O∪E
C = (I ∪ X ∪ A ∪ O, E) is an assignment D ∈ {0, 1}          of 0/1 labels to the input and
output gates, and to the wires E, with the following rules:

    1. for an input gate, the integer sum of the outgoing labels must be equal to the gate’s
       label;

    2. for a XOR gate, the integer sum of the incoming labels must equal the integer sum
       of the outgoing labels, and these sums must equal 0 or 1;

    3. for an AND gate, the integer sum of the outgoing wire labels must be equal to 0 if
       all incoming wire labels are 0, and 1 otherwise;

    4. for an output gate, its label must be equal to the incoming edge’s label.

Remark 1. The trail rules from [XZBL16] do not allow outdegree larger than 1 for XOR
and AND gates, but allow special COPY gates with indegree 1 and arbitrary positive
outdegree (or a 1-to-2 COPY gate which can be repeated to achieve the same effect).
Our description eliminates them by allowing arbitrary outdegrees and adapting the rules
accordingly. It is easy to verify that the definitions are equivalent.
Remark 2. We also note that the trail rules from [XZBL16] are optimized (compared to
the original rules from [Tod15, TM16]) by removing the so-called “redundant” transitions,
which are derived from non-redundant ones by switching any amount of output labels from
0 to 1.
    Division trail rules can be interpreted in the (maximum) network flow framework with
0/1 flows: a XOR gate simply limits the flow to 1 (and can be implemented in the standard
network flow by an edge with capacity 1); an AND gate is special: it allows to discard1
(or send directly to the sink) any flow above 1. As we will show, this special gate makes
the problem NP-hard, in contrast to the standard maximum flow problem which can be
easily solved in polynomial time.

Problem 1 (Division trail search [XZBL16]). Given a Boolean circuit C with XOR and
AND gates and one output gate, decide if there exists a division trail assigning 1 to all
input gates and to the output gate.
   1 In the context of our problem, discarding flow is always beneficial, that is why the AND rule we

describe only outputs at most one 1.

   Note that an AND gate can propagate any assignment of its incoming labels, while a
XOR gate requires that at most one incoming label is set to 1. The nondeterminism in the
propagation comes solely from “routing”: deciding which of the outgoing edges (if any)
needs to be set to 1.
Remark 3. This is the most minimalistic, monotone variant of the problem designed to
minimize the search space, following the optimizations from [XZBL16], focusing on all
input labels set to 1 and on a single output bit set to 1. One may allow additional 0-labeled
inputs and outputs, but these can be eliminated together with relevant parts of the circuit,
without changing the solvability of the instance.


3      NP-completeness of the two-subset division property
Theorem 1. Problem 1 is NP-complete.

the rules. We will reduce the CNF-SAT problem (Satisfiability of a CNF2 formula) to it

least one clause.

4                   Conventional bit-based division property trail search is NP-complete


    We will now construct a division trail search instance/circuit (see Figure 1). First, assign
an input gate to each of the clauses cj (m inputs). Second, create an AND node for each
variable xi and for its negation ¬xi (2n AND gates). We will identify these clauses/variable
labels with the corresponding gates. Then, connect each clause cj = {xi1 , . . . , ¬xk1 . . .}
with each of the variables or negations present in it:

                              cj → xi1 , . . . , cj → ¬xk1 , . . .

Third, create a XOR gate Xi for each variable xi (n XOR gates) and add wires from xi
and ¬xi to it:
                                xi → Xi , ¬xi → Xi .
Lastly, we add a final AND gate N , and wires Xi → N for all i, and wire N → o to the
only output gate o. Its purpose is only a formality to ensure a single output. The resulting
circuit is thus

                             C = (I ∪ X ∪ A ∪ O, E), where
                              I = {c1 , . . . , cm },
                             X = {X1 , . . . , Xn },
                             A = {x1 , . . . , xn , ¬x1 , . . . , ¬xn , N },
                             O = {o},

    We now prove that Problem 1 for this circuit has a solution if and only if the original
CNF formula is satisfiable.
    (CNF satisfiable ⇒ division trail exists) Consider a satisfying assignment for the formula.
For each clause cj , we choose arbitrarily the literal xi (or ¬xi ) which satisfies it in the
assignment, and assign label 1 to the corresponding edge; all other edges from cj are
assigned to 0. Since under a fixed satisfying CNF assignment only one of xi and ¬xi is
true, at most one of the corresponding AND gates in the circuit will receive a positive
number of nonzero incoming labels. Therefore, at most one of these two gates may have its
single output wire assigned the label 1. Therefore, the XOR gate Xi will have at most one
incoming wire labeled with 1, and its output wire is correctly and deterministically assigned.
Finally, it is easy to see that the output wire of the AND gate has to be (correctly) set
to 1, since no gate can completely eliminate all labels 1 from its input, and the circuit’s
inputs are labeled with 1.
    (division trail exists ⇒ CNF satisfiable) In a division trail, each XOR gate Xi cannot
have both incoming wires set to 1. Therefore, at most one of the AND gates xi , ¬xi have
a positive number of incoming wires and the outgoing wire labeled 1. If xi does, we set
the variable xi to 1. Otherwise, we set the variable xi to 0. For every input gate cj (which
is labeled 1 by the problem definition), there must be a single outgoing edge labeled 1 to
some gate xi /¬xi . This means that this gate was previously selected and the variable was
assigned. By the construction of the circuit edges cj → xi /¬xi , this variable assignment
satisfies this clause. We conclude that all the clauses must be satisfied with the assignment,
and the assignment is non-contradictory due to the discussion from the beginning of the
paragraph.

Discussion If one takes a hard CNF instance and construct the circuit as in the proof,
this should result in a hard division trail search instance (for MILP or any other solver).
The circuit in the proof has m inputs and 3n + 1 computational gates. For hard CNF
instances the circuit will have many inputs. The depth of the circuit is constant (three,
 Aleksei Udovenko                                                                                      5


counting XOR/AND gates only), although the first and the third layers use arbitrary
fan-in gates.
    While division property is difficult to evaluate over large binary linear layers [MWWZ22],
there are no complicated linear layers in the circuit from the reduction, the combinatorial
complexity clearly comes from routing the input labels 1 to the right literal xi /¬xi gates.
In the description from [XZW+ 24], the “routing” is implemented using the COPY gates,
and thus they are the main source of hardness in the proof.
    It is interesting that the weakest bit-based division property variant (2-subset) is
NP-complete, while the strongest one (monomial prediction) is not known to be such
(although it is known to be ⊕P -complete3 ). At the same time, there is no proof that
the ⊕P class contains NP (although probabilistic machines with an ⊕P oracle can solve
NP problems [For09]), so the situation with division property variants is similar to the
situation with the complexity classes.


4     Conclusion
The main consequence of this result is ruling out a generally efficient (for example,
maximum-flow-based) algorithm for the conventional 2-subset bit-based division property.
An interesting remaining question is understanding good performance of MILP solvers on
real-world instances, as well as their limits.
